title: Energy in SHM; Damping, forced oscillations and resonance
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: O04-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; O03-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; O03-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; O04-1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: O03-1#N.1a, O04-1#N.2a, O03-1#N.9a, O04-1#N.4a, O04-1#N.10a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Forced oscillation
items.clue: Motion kept going by a periodic driver, which sets its steady rate.

items.label: Turning point
items.clue: Either extreme, x = +A or x = –A, where the oscillator is momentarily at rest.

items.label: Total energy
items.clue: Sum that stays constant for an undamped oscillator: a horizontal line against x.

items.label: Natural frequency
items.clue: Symbol f₀: cycles per second of a system that is displaced, let go and left alone.

questions.stem: A mass on a horizontal spring moves with simple harmonic motion on a frictionless surface; air resistance is negligible. Which statement about the energy of the oscillator is correct?

options.text: At each extreme, E_k is greatest, because the acceleration of the mass is greatest there.
At each extreme, the total energy is zero, because the mass is not moving there.
At each extreme, all the energy is stored in the spring, because the mass is at rest.
The total energy falls during each cycle, because energy is used up in keeping the mass moving.

questions.stem: A lightly damped mass–spring system has a natural frequency of 2.0 Hz. It is driven by a periodic force of constant amplitude with a frequency of 3.5 Hz. Which describes its oscillation once the amplitude has become steady?

options.text: At 3.5 Hz, with a smaller amplitude than when driven at 2.0 Hz
At 2.0 Hz, its natural frequency, with a small steady amplitude
At 3.5 Hz, with a larger amplitude than when it is driven at 2.0 Hz
At 3.5 Hz, with the same amplitude as when it is driven at 2.0 Hz

questions.stem: A mass of 0.25 kg on a spring of spring constant 16 N m⁻¹ oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.050 m. What is its speed when its displacement is 0.030 m?
In its spin cycle, a washing machine's drum speeds up steadily. At one rotation rate the whole machine shakes violently; at higher rates it runs smoothly again. Why does it shake at that one rate?

options.text: It is then rotating fastest, so it transfers the most energy per second.
The rotation rate then equals a natural frequency of the machine.
The damping in the machine's mounts falls to zero at that rotation rate.
It is no longer forced: the machine now oscillates freely at its own frequency.

questions.explanation: The spinning drum drives the machine. When the driving frequency matches a natural frequency, energy builds up each cycle: resonance, maximum amplitude.

questions.stem: A singer shatters a wine glass by singing one steady note close to it. Which condition is essential for this to happen?

options.text: The note is very loud, whatever frequency the singer chooses.
The note is the highest frequency that the singer is able to produce.
The note's frequency is equal to a natural frequency of the glass.
The sound echoes inside the bowl of the glass and builds up.
